chapter: Films, Las Vegas and the union
title: Las Vegas in 1947 with Lena Horne at the Flamingo
summary: Callender recalls Bugsy Siegel, Cugat's band, the Dust Bowl lodging with Arnold Ross and Irving Ashby, and Black musicians using the back door.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You mentioned something a minute ago when I was changing the tapes about going to Las Vegas with Lena Horne. Tell me about that.
That was in 1947. The Flamingo... Did I mention the Last Frontier? But it was the Flamingo.
Well, you mentioned Bugsy Siegel, and Bugsy Siegel was connected with...

Well, Bugsy Siegel was the owner. At least he was supposed to have been the owner. And Xavier Cugat's band was featured, and was it Lynn René... I've forgotten who... Was that the name of the girl in that film we looked
at a minute ago? Anyhow, Xavier Cugat's was the featured orchestra...

Lena Romai(?). Xavier Cugat's band was the featured orchestra, and Lena Horne was the featured attraction. And she took Arnold Ross and Irving Ashby and myself. We were her trio. And we actually saw the incident which has been in a few books, where a waiter dropped a plate or made some noise, and Bugsy Siegel literally kicked the guy out of the room. And that was during... During that period in Las Vegas, Blacks couldn't stay on whatever side of town it was. We stayed over in a place called the Dust Bowl.
Was that the West Side. Well, wherever it was, that's where the Black musicians had to...
It was called the Dust Bowl the streets were not paved...

The streets were not paved, right. And we stayed at...I think the lady's house was Miss Harris. So Arnold Ross, who I love dearly, refused to stay... He could have stayed anywhere, but he decided he was going to stay with us, because we were together. So we all shared one room with I guess three beds in the room, but that's the

best we could do at that time. And Lena had... Well, they gave Lena a cabin or whatever you call it, a motor-home or something in back of the Flamingo. That's when things were really mean. You had to go in the back door... That is, the Black musicians had to go in the back door, and well, we were...
And stay in the back, yeah. When you got through, you couldn't go in the dining room. That's what being invisible means, I suppose.
